lead: Ponchon-Savarit designs binary distillation with an enthalpy-composition diagram instead of a y-x diagram. It drops the constant molar overflow assumption, so it handles unequal latent heats, concentrated solutions and large heat effects. Two curves, saturated-vapour enthalpy H against y and saturated-liquid enthalpy h against x, carry both material and energy balances. A fixed difference point for each section replaces the operating line. Chemical and petrochemical columns use this check when McCabe-Thiele is too rough.
prereq: You need: 4.1 VLE for equilibrium tie lines, 4.4 operating lines, and basic enthalpy balances from thermodynamics.

sections.h3: Two enthalpy curves and a fixed point

blocks.text: McCabe-Thiele assumes constant molar overflow: every mole of vapour condensing sends one mole of liquid down. That holds when the two components have equal latent heats and the column loses no heat. Real mixtures break this rule. Ponchon-Savarit keeps the energy balance honestly.

The diagram has two enthalpy curves. H is the enthalpy of saturated vapour in kJ per mole of mixture, plotted against vapour mole fraction y. h is the enthalpy of saturated liquid in kJ per mole of mixture, plotted against liquid mole fraction x. Both x and y refer to the more volatile component. The vertical gap H − h at equilibrium is the latent heat of vaporisation; it need not be constant.

A difference point replaces the operating line. For the rectifying section the point is Δ<sub>D</sub>. Its abscissa is the distillate composition x<sub>D</sub>. Its ordinate is an enthalpy H<sub>ΔD</sub>, found from the reflux ratio and the two enthalpy curves. All rectifying operating lines pass through Δ<sub>D</sub>. This single fixed point carries the section's material and energy balances together.

For the rectifying section, take an envelope from the top tray through the condenser. The vapour rate is V, the liquid reflux rate is L, and the distillate rate is D. The reflux ratio is R = L/D. When H<sub>V</sub> and h<sub>L</sub> do not change from tray to tray, the balance gives the ordinate of Δ<sub>D</sub>.

blocks.where: H<sub>ΔD</sub> is the ordinate of the rectifying difference point in kJ/mol; H<sub>V</sub> is the saturated-vapour enthalpy in kJ/mol; h<sub>L</sub> is the saturated-liquid reflux enthalpy in kJ/mol; R = L/D is the reflux ratio, with L the liquid returned to the column and D the distillate, both in mol/s.

blocks.text: The difference point is (x<sub>D</sub>, H<sub>ΔD</sub>). It is a construction point, not a tray. It usually sits above the saturated-vapour line because the condenser removes heat. A larger R raises H<sub>ΔD</sub>: more liquid reflux returns to the column, so more vapour must be condensed and the enthalpy difference grows.

items: Plot H against y and h against x on the same axes.
Start at the reflux liquid (x<sub>D</sub>, h<sub>L</sub>) on the h curve.
Join Δ<sub>D</sub> to that liquid point and extend the line to cut the H curve. The cut is the vapour leaving the top tray.
Draw the equilibrium tie line from that vapour point to the h curve. This gives the liquid leaving the tray, x<sub>1</sub>. Repeat with the new liquid point.

blocks.text: Each line from Δ<sub>D</sub> to a saturated-liquid point is the operating line for that tray. Its cut with the H curve gives the vapour entering that tray. The equilibrium tie line then moves to the liquid leaving the tray.

sections.h3: Stripping point and the McCabe-Thiele limit

blocks.text: The stripping section has its own difference point Δ<sub>B</sub> at x<sub>B</sub>, the bottoms composition. With constant H<sub>V</sub> and h<sub>L</sub>, its ordinate is H<sub>ΔB</sub> = h<sub>L</sub> − (V′/B)(H<sub>V</sub> − h<sub>L</sub>). Here V′ is the boil-up vapour rate and B is the bottoms rate, both mol/s. V′/B is the boil-up ratio. This point lies below the h curve. Stripping operating lines are straight lines through Δ<sub>B</sub>.

McCabe-Thiele is the special case of equal latent heats. Put H<sub>V</sub> and h<sub>L</sub> horizontal with constant gap λ = H<sub>V</sub> − h<sub>L</sub>. For a liquid point (x, h<sub>L</sub>), the line from Δ<sub>D</sub> cuts the H line at the y-x operating line.

blocks.where: y is the vapour mole fraction on the McCabe-Thiele operating line; x is the liquid mole fraction; R is the reflux ratio; xD is the distillate mole fraction. This is the rectifying line from 4.4.

blocks.text: So the y-x operating line returns. Real columns with sloped H or h curves need Ponchon-Savarit; columns with nearly constant enthalpies can use McCabe-Thiele.

figure.caption: The difference point for x<sub>D</sub> = 0.95, H<sub>V</sub> = 50 kJ/mol, h<sub>L</sub> = 20 kJ/mol and R = 2 sits at 110 kJ/mol, above the vapour line.

spec.aria: Enthalpy-composition plot with vapour and liquid lines and the rectifying difference point at x=0.95, enthalpy 110.

examples.question: A binary distillation column has a total condenser. The saturated-vapour enthalpy is H<sub>V</sub> = 50 kJ/mol and the saturated-liquid enthalpy is h<sub>L</sub> = 20 kJ/mol. Both stay constant over the working range. The distillate composition is x<sub>D</sub> = 0.95 mole fraction of the more volatile component. The reflux ratio is R = 2.0. Find the ordinate H<sub>ΔD</sub> of the rectifying difference point Δ<sub>D</sub>. State its coordinates on the enthalpy-composition diagram.
steps: Write the formula: H<sub>ΔD</sub> = H<sub>V</sub> + R(H<sub>V</sub> − h<sub>L</sub>).
Subtract the liquid enthalpy from the vapour enthalpy: H<sub>V</sub> − h<sub>L</sub> = 50 − 20 = 30 kJ/mol.
Multiply by the reflux ratio: R(H<sub>V</sub> − h<sub>L</sub>) = 2.0 × 30 = 60 kJ/mol.
Add the vapour enthalpy: H<sub>ΔD</sub> = 50 + 60 = 110 kJ/mol.
The coordinates are (x<sub>D</sub>, H<sub>ΔD</sub>) = (0.95, 110 kJ/mol). The point lies above the vapour line because 110 kJ/mol > 50 kJ/mol.
examples.answer: The rectifying difference point is at x = 0.95 and enthalpy 110 kJ/mol.
examples.check:
H_V = 50.0
h_L = 20.0
R = 2.0
H_delta = H_V + R * (H_V - h_L)
print(H_delta)

traps: Putting Δ<sub>D</sub> on the equilibrium curve. Δ<sub>D</sub> is fixed by x<sub>D</sub> and R; it is usually above the H curve.
Using H and h per mole of one component. They are per mole of mixture; a mole of mixture changes composition.
Writing R = L/V. The reflux ratio is R = L/D, and V = L + D.
Treating H<sub>ΔD</sub> as only condenser duty. H<sub>ΔD</sub> = H<sub>V</sub> + R(H<sub>V</sub> − h<sub>L</sub>) is an enthalpy difference per mole of distillate; it includes reflux enthalpy.
Placing Δ<sub>B</sub> above the h curve. It normally lies below because the reboiler adds heat.

quiz.q: What is plotted on the H-x and h-x curves of a Ponchon-Savarit diagram?
quiz.a: H-x gives saturated-vapour enthalpy against vapour mole fraction y. h-x gives saturated-liquid enthalpy against liquid mole fraction x. Both enthalpies are per mole of mixture.

quiz.q: Write the formula for H<sub>ΔD</sub> when H<sub>V</sub> and h<sub>L</sub> are constant.
quiz.a: H<sub>ΔD</sub> = H<sub>V</sub> + R(H<sub>V</sub> − h<sub>L</sub>), where R = L/D is the reflux ratio.

quiz.q: Why does Ponchon-Savarit not need the constant molar overflow assumption?
quiz.a: It carries an enthalpy balance with the material balance. The H and h curves allow the vapour and liquid rates to change from tray to tray as enthalpies change. McCabe-Thiele fixes the molar overflow, so it needs equal latent heats and no heat loss.

quiz.q: Use H<sub>V</sub> = 50 kJ/mol, h<sub>L</sub> = 20 kJ/mol, x<sub>D</sub> = 0.95 and R = 3.0. Find H<sub>ΔD</sub>.
quiz.a: H<sub>V</sub> − h<sub>L</sub> = 50 − 20 = 30 kJ/mol. R(H<sub>V</sub> − h<sub>L</sub>) = 3.0 × 30 = 90 kJ/mol. H<sub>ΔD</sub> = 50 + 90 = 140 kJ/mol. The point is (0.95, 140 kJ/mol).

quiz.q: For R = 2.0 and x<sub>D</sub> = 0.95, what are the slope and intercept of the McCabe-Thiele rectifying line in the equal-latent-heat limit?
quiz.a: Slope = R/(R+1) = 2.0/3.0 = 0.667. Intercept = x<sub>D</sub>/(R+1) = 0.95/3.0 = 0.317 mole fraction.

quiz.q: What happens to Δ<sub>D</sub> and the rectifying operating lines as R increases at fixed x<sub>D</sub>?
quiz.a: H<sub>ΔD</sub> increases because R(H<sub>V</sub> − h<sub>L</sub>) grows. Δ<sub>D</sub> moves upward on the H-x diagram. The operating lines through Δ<sub>D</sub> fan out, the y-x slope rises, and fewer stages are needed, but more reflux and more condenser duty are required.

quiz.q: A student draws Δ<sub>D</sub> at (0.95, 50) for H<sub>V</sub> = 50 kJ/mol, h<sub>L</sub> = 20 kJ/mol and R = 2. Explain the mistake and the correct ordinate.
quiz.a: The student used the vapour enthalpy H<sub>V</sub> = 50 kJ/mol as the ordinate and ignored the reflux term. The correct ordinate is H<sub>ΔD</sub> = 50 + 2(50 − 20) = 110 kJ/mol. The point should be (0.95, 110 kJ/mol), above the H line.

beyond: Not for the exam. Commercial flowsheeting software carries enthalpy-explicit VLE models and solves the same balances numerically, so Ponchon-Savarit is a visual check rather than a design tool. Researchers use enthalpy-composition diagrams for azeotropic and extractive distillation, where the solvent changes both equilibrium and enthalpy. Search next for 'enthalpy-composition diagram', 'Ponchon-Savarit graphical construction' and 'constant molar overflow assumption'.
